name: Terraform
license: Business Source License 1.1 since 1.6 (source-available, not OSI open source); MPL 2.0 before the August 2023 change
summary: The most widely used infrastructure-as-code tool: declare resources in HCL, review a plan, and apply it through provider plugins.
intro: You describe resources in `.tf` files written in HCL, HashiCorp’s configuration language. Terraform reads them, builds a dependency graph (the subnet needs the VPC first), and compares the result with its state file, a JSON record of every resource it created and its real ID. `terraform plan` lists what it will create, change or destroy; `terraform apply` then calls the cloud APIs, in parallel wherever the graph allows. Each API is reached through a provider plugin, and the Terraform Registry has thousands of them: AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Kubernetes, GitHub, DNS hosts and many more. That is the main difference from CloudFormation or Bicep: one tool and one workflow across every vendor.

In August 2023 HashiCorp moved Terraform from the open-source MPL 2.0 to the Business Source License 1.1. You can still use it free of charge, in production too; what the licence forbids is building it into a product that competes with HashiCorp, such as a hosted Terraform service. In response, a group of vendors forked the last MPL release as OpenTofu, which stays backward compatible with Terraform and is now a CNCF Sandbox project. IBM completed its acquisition of HashiCorp in February 2025. HCP Terraform is HashiCorp’s hosted service for remote state and runs: free for small teams, with paid editions for larger ones.
strengths: One language and workflow for every major cloud and hundreds of SaaS APIs, through providers on the Terraform Registry
`terraform plan` shows exactly what will be created, changed or destroyed before anything is touched
Huge ecosystem of reusable modules, examples and engineers who already know it
The S3 backend can lock state with a lock file in the bucket (`use_lockfile`), so no separate lock table is needed
limits: The state file is critical and can contain secrets in plain text; it has to live in a remote, locked, access-controlled backend
Changes made by hand in the console stay invisible until the next plan, and renaming or moving resources needs `moved` blocks or state surgery
No longer OSI open source: companies building a competing product need OpenTofu or a commercial agreement
HCL is declarative; complex logic with `count`, `for_each` and conditionals gets awkward compared with Pulumi or the AWS CDK
HashiCorp archived CDK for Terraform (CDKTF) in December 2025, so writing Terraform in TypeScript or Python is no longer supported

story: On February 25, 2011, AWS launched CloudFormation, which builds a whole stack of AWS resources from one JSON template, in the right order. The very next day Mitchell Hashimoto blogged that he was impressed by the idea, but that what was really needed was an open-source, cloud-agnostic solution: the same workflow whichever cloud you used. CloudFormation only knew AWS.

Nobody else built it, so three and a half years later Hashimoto’s company, HashiCorp, did. Terraform 0.1 came out on July 28, 2014, supporting only AWS and DigitalOcean. Downloads were mostly flat for the first 18 months, and the team even talked about shutting the project down. Then they began doubling every month, and in 2017 Microsoft became its first major cloud partner.

By version 1.0 in 2021 Terraform had been downloaded more than 100 million times and had over a thousand providers. In August 2023 HashiCorp moved it to the Business Source License, a group of companies forked the last open-source release as OpenTofu, and in February 2025 IBM completed its purchase of HashiCorp.

choices.why: Being cloud-agnostic meant the core could know nothing about any one API. Each cloud or service gets its own provider plugin, which is how one tool grew from two clouds to thousands of providers.
Terraform shows an execution plan of what it will create, change or destroy and acts only on approval, so infrastructure changes can be reviewed like code before anything is touched.

choices.choice: A state file as the record of what exists
choices.why: Mapping each resource in the code to a real ID lets Terraform work out the difference between configuration and reality, at the cost of a file that must be stored, locked and protected.

choices.choice: HCL instead of JSON or a programming language
choices.why: HashiCorp designed HCL as a compromise between a data format like JSON and configuration written in a full language like Ruby: easy for humans to read and write, declarative, with a JSON form for machines.

timeline.text: Hashimoto calls for an open, cloud-agnostic CloudFormation
Terraform 0.1 released in July with AWS and DigitalOcean
Terraform 1.0, after more than 100 million downloads
Relicensed under the BSL in August; OpenTofu fork follows
IBM completes its acquisition of HashiCorp in February
